title: Foundations: bounds & correctness
description: Start here: asymptotic notation, tightness, counting work, and the correctness proofs and loop invariants from your lectures.

topics.title: The five asymptotic notations
topics.summary: Before comparing algorithms, identify the input size n and the function f(n): it might count comparisons, printed stars, or runtime. Asymptotic notation describes growth for sufficiently large n, allowing fixed constant factors. It does not describe an exact running time in seconds.
points: Big-O: f(n)=O(g(n)) means there exist c>0 and n₀ such that 0≤f(n)≤cg(n) for all n≥n₀. This is an eventual upper bound.
Big-Omega: f(n)=Ω(g(n)) means there exist c>0 and n₀ such that 0≤cg(n)≤f(n) for all n≥n₀. This is an eventual lower bound.
Big-Theta: f(n)=Θ(g(n)) means there exist positive c₁,c₂ and n₀ such that c₁g(n)≤f(n)≤c₂g(n) for all n≥n₀. Both bounds describe the same function.
Little-o: f(n)=o(g(n)) means for every c>0 there exists n₀ such that 0≤f(n)<cg(n) for all n≥n₀. The threshold may depend on c. For positive g, this is equivalent to f(n)/g(n)→0.
Little-omega: f(n)=ω(g(n)) means for every c>0 there exists n₀ such that 0≤cg(n)<f(n) for all n≥n₀. For positive functions, f(n)/g(n)→∞. Equivalently, g=o(f).

When a ratio tends to a positive finite constant, the functions are Θ of each other. A ratio need not converge: a Θ bound can still hold without a limit. Use inequalities when the limit test is inconclusive.

excerpt.text: O(g(n)) = {f(n) : ∃c > 0, ∃n0 > 0 such that ∀n ≥ n0, 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ cg(n)}

topics.pitfall: Big-O is not a synonym for worst case, and Omega is not a synonym for best case. First specify the runtime function, then bound that function.
topics.example: For f(n)=2n and g(n)=n: f=O(g), f=Ω(g), and f=Θ(g). But f is neither o(g) nor ω(g), because f/g=2.

topics.title: Tight bounds and proofs with constants
topics.summary: A bound can be true without being tight. Saying a linear function is O(n²) gives a valid ceiling, but Θ(n) captures its actual growth. Tightness means you have matching upper and lower bounds, up to fixed positive constant factors.
points: For n≥1, 3n²≤3n²+4≤7n². Thus c₁=3,c₂=7,n₀=1 prove Θ(n²). This also implies O(n³), but not Θ(n³).
For 2n+1=O(n²), choose c=3,n₀=1: 2n+1≤3n≤3n². HW1 Q6 asks whether particular supplied pairs work, not whether any pair exists.

To disprove f=O(g), show no fixed multiplier can work eventually. If f/g→∞, it exceeds every proposed c at sufficiently large n. A counterexample to one pair alone does not disprove the entire Big-O claim.

Lecture 2 bounds fixed-loop bubble sort from both directions. There are at most n² comparisons. For even n, the first n/2 outer iterations each make at least n/2 comparisons, giving at least n²/4. Floors change only constants. Therefore the count is Θ(n²).
Tight bounds do not give an exact count. Θ(n²) includes n², 7n²+4n, and n(n−1)/2. An exact-answer question still requires the requested expression.

excerpt.text: Since runtime is both O(n 2) and Ω(n 2), it is θ(n 2)

topics.pitfall: The proof must bound the same quantity on both sides. An upper bound for worst case and a lower bound for a different function are not automatically a Θ proof.
topics.example: For n²+7n+5, division by n gives n+7+5/n→∞. Therefore it is not O(n), although checking a few small inputs might suggest otherwise.

topics.title: Count work before choosing a bound
topics.summary: Runtime analysis begins with a cost model: decide which operation you count. HW1 counts printed asterisks and element comparisons. A loop-condition check, a swap, and an element comparison are different events; exact-count questions need this distinction.
points: Sequential loops add: n prints followed by n−1 prints give 2n−1=Θ(n).
Nested loops with a fixed inner count multiply: n outer iterations with n−1 prints each give n(n−1)=Θ(n²).
If the inner count is i, sum over i: Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ i=n(n+1)/2. Do not replace every iteration by its largest size when an exact answer is required.
The upper endpoint is part of the formula. Summing integers through n² gives n²(n²+1)/2=Θ(n⁴), not Θ(n²).

In descending-input insertion sort, iteration i compares the key to i−1 preceding values. Sum from i=2 through n to get n(n−1)/2. When j=0, short-circuit evaluation stops at j>0, so A[j]>key is not evaluated again.

excerpt.text: Never forget, the sum of the numbers from 1 to n is

topics.pitfall: Two nested loops need not take Θ(n²): inspect their ranges and the cost of each body. Logarithmic ranges, dependent bounds, and early exits change the count.
topics.example: For n=4, insertion sort on [12,8,7,3] makes 1+2+3=6 element comparisons. The sum through n would incorrectly give 10.

topics.title: Correctness and the loop-invariant template
topics.summary: Correctness means satisfying a specification for every permitted input. A precondition states what is assumed initially. A postcondition states what must hold at the end. For sorting, the output must be ordered and must preserve the original values, including duplicates.
points: Initialization: substitute the first loop index into the invariant and prove it. An empty prefix often makes a universally quantified statement vacuously true.

Maintenance: assume the invariant at the start of an arbitrary iteration; analyze every branch of the body and prove the invariant at the next checkpoint. Update the index in the statement, not just the array.

Termination: explain why execution stops. A bounded counter increasing toward its limit, or a nonnegative integer decreasing each step, can justify this. For nested loops, justify termination of the inner loop too.

Conclusion: substitute the exit index and combine the invariant with the exit condition to obtain the postcondition. An invariant alone need not be strong enough: “the array has length n” says nothing about sortedness.

Partial correctness says that if execution terminates, its result satisfies the specification. Total correctness additionally establishes termination. This terminology is a study explanation of the lecture’s proof obligations.

Testing can refute an invariant with one input and checkpoint. It cannot prove a universal claim just by succeeding on examples. HW1 Q8 deliberately includes properties that fail only at the final checkpoint.

excerpt.text: Show true before first iteration of loop.

topics.pitfall: Do not assume the result you are trying to prove. Maintenance may assume only the current invariant and stated preconditions.
topics.example: For “for i=1 to n: A[i]=3”, use “A[1:i−1] is all 3s”. It holds initially for an empty prefix, grows by one assignment, and at exit i=n+1 describes the entire array.

topics.title: Bubble sort: the lecture’s full invariant proof
topics.summary: The lecture’s bubble sort scans its inner loop from right to left. Each outer iteration moves the smallest remaining value into the next position of a growing sorted prefix. Fix that direction before writing a proof: a different scan direction needs a different invariant.
points: Initialization (i=1): the prefix A[1:0] is empty. It contains the zero smallest values in sorted order; all original values remain in A[1:n].

Inner-loop reasoning: before comparing A[j−1] and A[j], A[j] is a smallest value of the suffix A[j:n]. This is initially true at j=n. Comparing and possibly swapping places a smallest value of A[j−1:n] into A[j−1], so the property advances left.

Maintenance: by the time j reaches i+1, the smallest value of A[i:n] moves to A[i]. The earlier prefix is untouched. Since it already contains the i−1 smallest original values, appending the next smallest makes A[1:i] the sorted prefix required for the next outer checkpoint i+1.
Preservation: only swaps occur, so the multiset of values stays identical to the input. The unprocessed suffix contains exactly the values outside the sorted prefix.
Termination: for each i the inner counter j decreases to i; the outer counter increases from 1 to n−1. Both loops have finite ranges.
Conclusion (exit i=n): A[1:n−1] contains the n−1 smallest values in sorted order. The remaining value in A[n] is largest. Hence the whole array is sorted and contains the original values.

excerpt.text: A[1 : i − 1] contains i − 1 smallest elements of original A, in sorted order, and A[i:n] contains the rest

topics.pitfall: Do not use “the prefix is sorted” alone: you also need that it contains the globally smallest values to conclude the final remaining value belongs at the end.
topics.example: [7,16,5,25] → [5,7,16,25] after the first right-to-left pass. The proof only requires the first position to be final at that point, even if the entire example happens to be sorted.

topics.title: Insertion sort: a proof using HW1’s checkpoints
topics.summary: Insertion sort maintains an ordered collection of the values processed so far. Unlike bubble sort’s prefix, these need not be the globally smallest input values. Save the next key, shift larger preceding values right, then insert the key into the gap.
points: Invariant at the start of outer iteration i: A[1:i−1] is a sorted permutation of A₀[1:i−1], and A[i:n]=A₀[i:n]. The unprocessed suffix has not changed.
Initialization (i=2): the prefix contains only A₀[1], which is already sorted. The remaining suffix equals the input suffix.

Maintenance: save key=A[i]. Every shifted value is greater than key. Because the prefix was sorted, moving these values one place right preserves their relative order. Stop when j=0 or A[j]≤key; inserting key at j+1 creates a sorted prefix containing precisely the first i original values.

Value preservation during shifting requires the saved key. The array alone can temporarily contain a duplicate while the missing value is held in key. At the outer checkpoint, insertion restores the original multiset.
Termination: each inner iteration decreases j, which cannot remain positive indefinitely. The outer loop advances through i=n and exits at i=n+1.
Conclusion: substituting i=n+1 into the invariant says A[1:n] is a sorted permutation of the original input. The required postcondition holds.

excerpt.text: Detailed analysis of Bubble Sort [book does Insertion Sort]

topics.pitfall: Do not claim the first i−1 entries are the globally smallest input values. In [12,8,7,3], the initial prefix [12] is sorted but contains the largest value.
topics.example: Before successive outer iterations: i=2 [12 | 8,7,3]; i=3 [8,12 | 7,3]; i=4 [7,8,12 | 3]; exit i=5 [3,7,8,12 |].

topics.title: Mergesort: recursive correctness and the merge invariant
topics.summary: A recursive correctness proof assumes correctness only for smaller inputs, then proves the current input is handled correctly. Lecture 3 gives three obligations: the base case, dividing the work correctly, and combining correct recursive results correctly.
points: Base case: a subarray with zero or one value is already sorted and is unchanged, so both ordering and value preservation hold.
Division and induction hypothesis: the two halves are disjoint and cover the input. Each has smaller length when n>1. By strong induction, each recursive call returns its own values in sorted order.

Merge invariant: before each comparison, the output prefix contains exactly the values consumed from the two halves, in sorted order; each output value is at most every unconsumed value. The indices point to the first unconsumed value of each half.
Merge initialization: the output prefix is empty, neither half is consumed, and both indices point to their beginnings.
Merge maintenance: each half is sorted, so a smallest remaining value is at one of the two fronts. Append the smaller front and advance only its index. All invariant clauses continue to hold.

Merge termination and conclusion: each step consumes a value. When one half is exhausted, append the other half’s already-sorted remainder, whose values are at least the output prefix. Every input value appears once, and the whole output is sorted.
Recursive termination: subproblem lengths strictly decrease until the base case. Together with the finite merge, this proves total correctness for mergesort.

excerpt.text: Assuming the recursive calls are correct, their results are combined correctly

topics.pitfall: The induction hypothesis does not prove the combine step for you. Two correctly sorted halves do not automatically form one correctly sorted concatenation.
topics.example: [2,6] and [1,5]: output [] → [1] → [1,2] → [1,2,5], then append 6. Each prefix is sorted and no unused value is smaller than its last value.

topics.title: Max-Heapify and Build-Max-Heap correctness
topics.summary: A max-heap is a complete binary tree where each parent is at least as large as its children. In its one-based array representation, children of index i are 2i and 2i+1 when those indices are within the heap. A leaf is automatically a max-heap.
points: Why Max-Heapify works: if the node is at least both children, the precondition makes the whole subtree a heap. Otherwise swap it with its larger child. That child was at least every value below it, so the promoted value is now at least both child roots.

Only the subtree receiving the old parent can now violate heap order, and its child subtrees are still heaps. Repair it recursively. Inducting on subtree height proves the repair works. Each recursive call goes down one level, so it terminates at a leaf.
Build invariant: at the start of iteration i, every node with index greater than i is the root of a max-heap.
Initialization (i=⌊n/2⌋): all greater indices are leaves. Every one already satisfies the heap property.

Maintenance: existing children have indices greater than i, so their subtrees are heaps. Max-Heapify’s precondition holds. Its completed repair makes the entire subtree at i a heap, including its descendants; nodes outside that subtree are unchanged. Thus every index ≥i roots a heap at the next checkpoint i−1.

Termination and conclusion: i decreases by one and exits at 0. The invariant then includes node 1, so the entire array is a max-heap. Swaps preserve the input multiset. Empty arrays are handled vacuously.

excerpt.text: Loop Invariant: At start of each iteration of for-loop, nodes i+1 through n are all roots of Max-Heaps

topics.pitfall: Processing from the root downward does not establish the repair precondition: the child subtrees may still be unordered.
topics.example: With n=7, indices 4–7 start as one-node heaps. Repair index 3, then 2, then 1. The root is processed only after both of its child subtrees have been repaired.

topics.title: Heapsort: heap prefix and sorted suffix
topics.summary: Heapsort first builds a max-heap, then repeatedly swaps the maximum at the root into the last active position, shrinks the heap, and repairs its root. The array has two regions whose relationship is essential to the proof.
points: Initialization (i=n): Build-Max-Heap makes A[1:n] a max-heap. The suffix A[n+1:n] is empty and therefore sorted. The boundary-order condition is vacuous.
Maintenance, placing the maximum: the root is the largest prefix value. Swap it with A[i]. It is at least all values remaining in A[1:i−1] and at most every old suffix value, so A[i:n] is now sorted.

Maintenance, restoring the heap: shrink the heap size to i−1. Only the replacement root may violate heap order; its child subtrees remain heaps. Max-Heapify restores the heap without touching the sorted suffix. The invariant now holds for the next active size.
Preservation: the algorithm only swaps values, so no original value is lost or duplicated. Heap size describes the active region, not the physical array length.

Termination and conclusion: the active size decreases until it reaches 1. The one-element prefix is sorted, the suffix is sorted, and the prefix value is at most the suffix values. Thus the whole array is sorted. Arrays of size zero or one need no extraction.

excerpt.text: Heap only contains A[1…i]. They are the smallest items in A. Remaining elements are in A[i+1…n] in sorted order

topics.pitfall: Shrink heap size before repair. If repair is allowed to inspect the sorted suffix, the invariant can be destroyed.
topics.example: [4,2,3,1] → swap/shrink [1,2,3 | 4] → repair [3,2,1 | 4]. The invariant is required at iteration boundaries, not in the middle before repair finishes.

topics.title: Partition and Quicksort correctness
topics.summary: Partitioning orders values relative to a pivot, not relative to every other value. In the lecture’s one-based version, save x=A[n], scan j from 1 to n−1, and use i to mark the end of the low region. Initially i=0.
points: Initialization (j=1,i=0): both processed regions are empty; all non-pivot values are unprocessed. The invariant holds.
Maintenance when A[j]>x: leave it in place. Advancing j incorporates that value into the high region; the low region is unchanged.

Maintenance when A[j]≤x: increment i and swap A[i] with A[j]. The current value joins the low region. If i<j, the displaced value came from the old high region and remains high at position j; if i=j, the swap is with itself. Then advance j.
Exit (j=n): every non-pivot value has been classified. Swap A[i+1] with A[n]. The pivot ends at q=i+1, with all values to its left ≤x and all values to its right >x. Swaps preserve the multiset.

Quicksort correctness: use strong induction on subarray length. Lengths 0 and 1 are already sorted. Partition puts the pivot between the two regions; recursively sorting those strictly smaller regions yields a sorted whole, with every original value preserved.

Termination: the scan advances to n. Each recursive call excludes the pivot and has smaller length, even for a maximally unbalanced split. Correctness does not imply efficiency: equal values still cause quadratic runtime with this partition.

excerpt.text: Loop for j=1 to n-1, maintain invariant that the prefix A[1…j-1] of A is partitioned according to pivot

topics.pitfall: Do not claim the low and high regions are internally sorted. Partition establishes only their relationship to the pivot.
topics.example: For [4,2,3,8,9,1,7,5], x=5. Before j=6, i=3: [4,2,3 | 8,9 | 1,7 | 5]. Processing 1 increments i to 4 and swaps it with 8, giving [4,2,3,1 | 9,8 | 7 | 5].

topics.title: Induction: correctness versus runtime bounds
topics.summary: Induction is the common proof pattern behind loop invariants and recursive algorithms. State a proposition P(n), prove the base cases, assume smaller cases, then prove the current one. Weak induction assumes the preceding case; strong induction assumes all smaller cases in the stated domain.
points: Lecture 4’s warm-up: prove n!<nⁿ for n≥2. Base n=2: 2<4. For n>2, the hypothesis gives (n−1)!<(n−1)ⁿ⁻¹; multiplying by n gives n!<n(n−1)ⁿ⁻¹≤n·nⁿ⁻¹=nⁿ.
Runtime example from Lecture 4: T(1)=1 and T(n)=2T(⌊n/2⌋)+n for n>1. Prove the explicit inequality T(n)≤5n log₂ n for n≥2; keep the same constant in every recursive use.
Base cases: T(2)=4≤10 and T(3)=5≤15 log₂3. Both are necessary for this hypothesis because ⌊3/2⌋=1 is outside its domain n≥2.
Strong hypothesis: assume T(k)≤5k log₂k for every 2≤k<n. For n≥4, set m=⌊n/2⌋, so 2≤m<n. Then T(n)≤10m log₂m+n≤5n log₂(n/2)+n=5n log₂n−4n≤5n log₂n.
This establishes an O(n log n) upper bound, not a tight bound by itself. A matching lower bound is a separate task. The proof’s recursive arguments must always fall inside the hypothesis domain.
Loop maintenance is induction on the number of completed iterations. Recursive correctness typically uses strong induction on input size, since calls may use n/2 rather than n−1.

excerpt.text: Important not to use asymptotic notation in the inductive hypothesis!

topics.pitfall: Writing T(n)=2O(n/2)+O(n)=O(n) can hide constants that grow with recursion depth. Substitute a single explicit bound and show the same constant survives.
topics.example: At n=3 the recursive argument is 1. Since 5·1·log₂1=0<T(1)=1, the proposed bound does not hold there. Adding n=3 as a base case repairs the induction domain.

topics.title: Optional lecture extension: radix-sort invariant
topics.summary: Lecture 10 asks “Why does this work? Loop invariant?” for least-significant-digit radix sort. This lesson completes that proof prompt. The annotated old exam excludes radix sort and stability questions from Fall 2026 Exam 1; this extension is included for lecture-proof coverage, not restored exam practice.
points: Invariant at the start of pass i: the list is sorted by its lowest i−1 digits, viewed together as one numerical key. All original items are preserved.
Initialization (i=1): zero digits have been processed. Every item has the same empty key, so any order satisfies the invariant.

Maintenance: sorting on digit i orders groups by that digit. Within each equal-digit group, stability preserves the earlier order by the lowest i−1 digits. Thus the result is sorted by the lowest i digits, establishing the invariant for pass i+1.
Termination and conclusion: after d finite digit-sort passes, the exit checkpoint is i=d+1. The invariant says the list is sorted by all d digits, hence by the full key.

Why stability matters: an unstable digit sort can scramble the lower-digit order within an equal current-digit group. The inductive step would no longer follow. These details are a prepared solution to the lecture’s prompt.

excerpt.text: Why does this work? Loop invariant?

topics.pitfall: This proof assumes each digit pass is stable. Merely sorting the current digit is insufficient.
topics.example: For [12,11,22,21], a stable units pass gives [11,21,12,22]. A stable tens pass gives [11,12,21,22]. An unstable tens pass could leave [12,11,22,21], which is not numerically sorted.

title: Sorting algorithms
description: Seven ways to order a sequence: invariants, recurrences, and the cost of choosing a pivot.

topics.title: Bubblesort
topics.summary: Repeated adjacent comparisons move the next smallest element into the sorted prefix.
points: The lecture scans the inner loop from right to left. After outer iteration i, A[1:i] contains the i smallest elements in order.
With fixed loops, both sorted and reverse-sorted inputs take Θ(n²) time. Stable when equal elements are not swapped; in-place.
topics.example: [7,16,5,25] → [5,7,16,25] after the first full right-to-left pass.

excerpt.text: A[1 : i − 1] contains i − 1 smallest elements of original A, in sorted order

topics.pitfall: Do not claim the fixed-loop lecture version has a linear best case; that requires an early-exit modification.

topics.title: Insertion Sort
topics.summary: Insert each new element into an already sorted prefix. Study supplement: these slides refer to the textbook for insertion sort.
points: Before iteration j, A[1:j−1] is sorted; save A[j], shift larger values one position right, then insert the saved key.
Best case Θ(n), worst case Θ(n²). Stable with strict > in the shift test; in-place.
topics.example: [4,2,3] → [2,4,3] → [2,3,4]. In the second insertion, only 4 shifts.

excerpt.text: Detailed analysis of Bubble Sort [book does Insertion Sort]

topics.pitfall: Keep the key in a temporary variable before shifting, or its value is overwritten.

topics.title: Mergesort
topics.summary: Split in half, recursively sort each half, then merge two sorted lists.
points: Merge repeatedly takes the smaller front element from the two sorted halves in Θ(n) total time.
Θ(n log n) runtime. Standard array implementation uses Θ(n) auxiliary space; stable when ties come from the left half first.
topics.example: [8,3,5,1] splits into [8,3] and [5,1]; sort to [3,8] and [1,5]; merge to [1,3,5,8].

excerpt.text:
Divide array in half
Recursively sort both sides
Merge the two sorted sides

topics.pitfall: Merging is linear, not constant time. Include the work done outside recursive calls.

topics.title: Heapsort
topics.summary: Build a max-heap, then place its maximum at the end of the remaining heap repeatedly.
points: The array has two regions: an active max-heap prefix and a sorted suffix.
Build-Max-Heap costs Θ(n); n−1 removals and repairs cost O(n log n). Worst-case total Θ(n log n); in-place, generally unstable.
topics.formula: Θ(n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n); worst case Θ(n log n)

excerpt.text: Uses Build-Heap instead of inserting elements into heap one by one

topics.pitfall: Decrease heap size before heapifying; otherwise the sorted suffix can be pulled back into the heap.
topics.pseudocode:
Build-Max-Heap(A,n)
for j = n downto 2:
  swap(A[1],A[j])
  A.heapsize = A.heapsize − 1
  Max-Heapify(A,1)

topics.title: Generic Priority Queue sort
topics.summary: Insert all input elements into a separate max-priority queue, then extract maxima into the array from right to left.
points: This is an algorithm template: its runtime depends on the priority queue implementation.
Unsorted linked-list PQ: Θ(n²) total. Binary-heap PQ: Θ(n log n) worst-case total.
topics.formula: Total = n insertions + n Extract-Max operations
topics.example: Input [2,9,4]: extract 9 into A[3], 4 into A[2], 2 into A[1], obtaining [2,4,9].

excerpt.text: Insert elements of A into a PQ // Don’t change array A

topics.pitfall: Writing extracted maxima left to right produces descending order, not ascending order.

topics.title: Quicksort
topics.summary: Partition around a pivot, then recursively sort the elements on its two sides.
points: Partition runs in Θ(n) and puts the pivot in its final sorted position. The two sides need not themselves be sorted yet.
Balanced splits give Θ(n log n). Choosing the last element on sorted distinct input gives Θ(n²). Standard in-place partitioning is not stable.
topics.example: [4,2,8,3,9,1,7,5], pivot 5: the low side contains {1,2,3,4}, then 5, then {7,8,9}. Recurse on the two sides.

excerpt.text: Pick an element x of the array. Call it the “pivot”

topics.pitfall: Exclude the pivot from both recursive calls. Partitioning alone does not sort either side.

topics.title: Randomized-Quicksort
topics.summary: Choose the pivot uniformly at random in every recursive subarray.
points: For distinct sorted ranks z₁<…<zₙ, zᵢ and zⱼ are compared iff the first pivot from ranks i through j is one of the endpoints.
Expected Θ(n log n) time for every fixed distinct-key input. An unlucky execution can still take Θ(n²).
topics.formula: P(zᵢ compared with zⱼ) = 2/(j−i+1); E[C] = Σᵢ<ⱼ 2/(j−i+1)
topics.example: Ranks 2 and 5 are compared with probability 2/4 = 1/2: whichever of ranks 2,3,4,5 becomes a pivot first decides.

excerpt.text: We will prove that expected runtime of Randomized Quicksort is θ(n log n)

topics.pitfall: The expectation is over pivot choices, not a random input distribution. Naive two-way partitioning needs care with many equal keys.

title: Decision tree lower bounds
description: Why every comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.

topics.title: The Ω(n log n) sorting lower bound
topics.summary: A comparison sorting algorithm must distinguish all n! possible orders of distinct keys.
points: Each internal decision-tree node is a comparison; its two branches are possible outcomes for distinct keys. Each leaf fixes an output ordering.
At least n! leaves are necessary. A binary tree of height h has at most 2ʰ leaves, hence h≥log₂(n!).
Because log₂(n!)=Θ(n log n), some input needs Ω(n log n) comparisons. Mergesort and heapsort match this asymptotically.
topics.example: For n=4, there are 24 orders. Height 4 permits only 16 leaves, so at least one input requires ≥5 comparisons.

excerpt.text: There must be one leaf for every possible permutation of elements of A

topics.pitfall: This is a worst-case lower bound in the comparison model. It does not rule out counting sort using key values directly.

title: Mathematical toolkit
description: Growth rates, logarithmic depth, and the sums behind algorithm analysis.

topics.title: Asymptotic notation
topics.summary: Compare growth rates while ignoring fixed multiplicative constants and a finite initial range.
points: O is an eventual upper bound; Ω is an eventual lower bound; Θ means both.
For eventually positive functions: f=o(g) if f/g→0, and f=ω(g) if f/g→∞.
An O bound need not be tight. Θ is the appropriate notation when both bounds have been proved.
topics.example: 3n²+7n+4 is Θ(n²), O(n³), and o(n³). It is not Θ(n³).

excerpt.text: Remove lower order terms and multiplicative constants

topics.pitfall: O is not synonymous with worst case: you can express best-, average-, or worst-case functions using O.

topics.title: Logarithms
topics.summary: A logarithm answers how many times a base must multiply itself to reach a value.
points: For fixed bases greater than 1, changing the base changes only a constant factor.
A logarithm turns products into sums and powers into multipliers. It does not turn sums into sums of logs.
topics.formula: log_b x = ln x / ln b; log_b(xy)=log_b x+log_b y; log_b(xᵏ)=k log_b x
topics.example: log₂ 32=5; log₂(n²)=2 log₂ n; log₂ n and log₁₀ n are Θ of one another.

excerpt.text: change of base formula

topics.pitfall: log(a+b) is generally not log a + log b. Also, (log n)² and log(n²) grow differently.

topics.title: Repeated halving and doubling
topics.summary: Multiplicative changes lead to a logarithmic number of steps.
points: After k halvings, size is n/2ᵏ. Set this equal to 1 to find the depth.
After k doublings from 1, size is 2ᵏ. Reaching at least n requires ⌈log₂ n⌉ doublings.
topics.example: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 takes 6 halvings. A recursion tree has 7 levels if the root is level 0.

excerpt.text: How many days until you are down to only $1?

topics.pitfall: Distinguish the number of edges/halvings from the number of levels, which includes the starting level.

topics.title: Geometric series
topics.summary: When each term is a fixed multiple of the previous one, the ratio tells you which levels dominate.
points: For fixed r>1, a finite positive sum is Θ of its last term. For fixed 0≤r<1, it is Θ of its first term.
When r=1, multiply the common term by the number of terms. An infinite geometric series converges only when |r|<1.
topics.formula: Σᵢ₌₀ᵏ arⁱ = a(rᵏ⁺¹−1)/(r−1), r≠1; Σᵢ₌₀∞ arⁱ = a/(1−r), |r|<1

excerpt.text: finite geometric series

topics.pitfall: A finite geometric sum and an infinite one have different formulas. Include the i=0 term and count k+1 terms.

topics.title: Harmonic series
topics.summary: The first n reciprocals grow logarithmically even though each new term becomes smaller.
points: The infinite harmonic series diverges. Its finite partial sum Hₙ is Θ(log n).
Grouping terms into blocks [2ᵏ,2ᵏ⁺¹−1] gives Θ(1) per block and Θ(log n) blocks.
topics.example: H₄=1+1/2+1/3+1/4=25/12. In randomized quicksort, sums of reciprocal rank distances produce log n.

excerpt.text: Does this series converge? No.

topics.pitfall: Terms approaching zero do not imply the infinite series converges.

topics.title: Sum of numbers from 1 to n
topics.summary: Pair the first and last terms to turn a growing sum into a closed formula.
points: Each pair from opposite ends sums to n+1. There are n/2 pairs, allowing the middle term when n is odd.
Triangular loops often perform this many iterations.
topics.example: 1+2+3+4+5 = 5·6/2 = 15. Bubblesort comparisons stop at n−1, giving n(n−1)/2.

excerpt.text: Never forget, the sum of the numbers from 1 to n is

topics.pitfall: Check the endpoint: summing to n−1 changes the exact answer even though the Θ bound stays quadratic.

topics.title: The sum of i/2ⁱ
topics.summary: Exponential decay dominates the linear numerator, so the infinite sum is a constant.
points: Differentiate Σxⁱ=1/(1−x) and multiply by x to obtain Σixⁱ=x/(1−x)².
Substitute x=1/2. This sum also bounds the aggregate cost of Build-Max-Heap.

excerpt.text: Differentiate both sides wrt x, get

topics.pitfall: The finite sum is less than 2, not exactly 2. The equality to 2 applies to the infinite sum.

title: Probability
description: Turn repeated trials and event counts into expectations.

topics.title: Expected flips until heads
topics.summary: For independent trials with success probability p, the expected waiting time for the first success is 1/p.
points: For a fair coin, P(X=k)=(1/2)ᵏ: k−1 tails followed by one head. Therefore E[X]=Σk/2ᵏ=2.
A first-step equation gives E[X]=1+(1−p)E[X], so E[X]=1/p.
If flips are capped at m, use Σᵢ₌₁ᵐ (1−p)ⁱ⁻¹ instead.
topics.example: Stop on heads or after 4 flips: expected flips = 1+1/2+1/4+1/8 = 15/8.

excerpt.text: Expected number of trials to get first success is 1/p

topics.pitfall: Include the successful flip. For a cap of 4, P(X=4)=1/8 because both TTTH and TTTT stop after 4 flips.

topics.title: Indicator random variables
topics.summary: Represent an event by 1 when it occurs and 0 otherwise, then sum indicators to count events.
points: If I is an indicator for event E, E[I]=P(E).
Linearity says E[ΣIᵢ]=ΣE[Iᵢ], even when the indicators are dependent.
Pick the event carefully: the indicator that flip i occurs is different from the indicator that flip i is heads.
topics.example: With at most 4 flips until heads, I₃=1 exactly when the first two flips are tails, so E[I₃]=1/4.

excerpt.text:
Y = 1 if event occurs
Y = 0 if event does not occur

topics.pitfall: Independence is not required for linearity of expectation. It is required for certain product probability calculations.

title: Recurrence relations
description: Translate recursive work into a bound, then justify the bound.

topics.title: Master Theorem — the course version
topics.summary: The lecture theorem applies to equal-size subproblems and a polynomial nonrecursive term.
points: Assume T(n)=aT(n/b)+Θ(nᵈ), constant-size base cost Θ(1), and constants a>0, b>1, d≥0.
Compare d with log_b a. Smaller d means leaves dominate; equality means every level contributes equally; larger d means root work dominates.
This version does not directly cover a toll n log n or unequal splits T(n/3)+T(2n/3). Use another method.
topics.formula:
d<log_b a: Θ(n^(log_b a))
d=log_b a: Θ(nᵈ log n)
d>log_b a: Θ(nᵈ)
topics.example: 3T(n/2)+n: d=1<log₂3 → Θ(n^(log₂3)). 2T(n/2)+n → Θ(n log n). 2T(n/2)+n² → Θ(n²).

excerpt.text: a, b, d, n0 are constants

topics.pitfall: Do not use a more general textbook case to claim this course theorem directly handles n log n tolls. Floors/ceilings are accommodated as explained on lecture page 29.

topics.title: Recursion tree analysis
topics.summary: Draw the recursive calls, label only the local work at each node, and sum across all levels.
points: At depth i for aT(n/b)+cnᵈ, there are aⁱ nodes of size n/bⁱ. Local work for the whole level is cnᵈ(a/bᵈ)ⁱ.
Depth is log_b n for powers of b; there are a^(log_b n)=n^(log_b a) leaves. Include their base costs.
topics.formula: Level i work = cnᵈ(a/bᵈ)ⁱ; total = internal-level sum + leaf costs
topics.example: T(n)=2T(n/2)+n, T(1)=1: log₂ n internal levels each cost n, and n leaves cost n; T(n)=n log₂ n+n.

excerpt.text: Method 1: Using Recursion Tree to Solve Recurrence

topics.pitfall: Do not label a node with both T(size) and its local cost when summing; that counts recursive work twice.

topics.title: Solving recurrences by induction
topics.summary: Guess a concrete inequality, prove enough base cases, and substitute the inductive hypothesis.
points: Use an explicit constant in the hypothesis, such as T(k)≤ck log₂k. Big-O notation hides the constant you need to preserve.
Check every recursive argument is covered by the hypothesis. Floors may require more than one base case.
For an exact solution on powers of 2, prove T(n)=n log₂n+n by substituting the half-size formula.
topics.example: Base n=1: 1=1·0+1. For n>1, the displayed substitution establishes the formula for 2T(n/2)+n.

excerpt.text: Important not to use asymptotic notation in the inductive hypothesis!

topics.pitfall: Proving 2·O(n/2)+O(n)=O(n) does not prove T(n)=O(n): the implicit constant can increase at every recursion level.

title: Other algorithms
description: Two divide-and-conquer examples with very different recurrences.

topics.title: Maximum-sum subarray
topics.summary: Find the largest sum of a contiguous segment. In this course, the empty subarray is allowed and has sum 0.
points: An optimum lies wholly left, wholly right, or crosses the midpoint.
A crossing segment combines the maximum-sum suffix of the left half and maximum-sum prefix of the right half. Each can be scanned in linear time.
Brute-force recomputation takes Θ(n³); reusing running sums gives Θ(n²); the lecture divide-and-conquer algorithm gives Θ(n log n).
topics.example: [3,−6,2,3,−5,1,3,−7] has maximum sum 5, achieved by [2,3]. For [−4,−2], the course answer is 0 (empty subarray).

excerpt.text: The empty subarray is also considered to be a subarray. Sum of its elements is 0.

topics.pitfall: A subarray must be contiguous. Ignoring crossing subarrays makes the divide-and-conquer algorithm incorrect.

topics.title: Karatsuba’s algorithm
topics.summary: Multiply two long integers using three recursive products instead of four.
points: Write x=x_L·B+x_R and y=y_L·B+y_R, where B=2^(n/2).
Compute p=x_Ly_L, q=x_Ry_R, r=(x_L+x_R)(y_L+y_R). The cross term is r−p−q.
Additions, subtractions and shifts take Θ(n) bit operations; the lecture recurrence suppresses small carry/rounding details.

excerpt.text: Recursively compute 3 products instead of 4

topics.pitfall: The speedup is in bit-operation complexity for long integers. Treating arbitrary-length multiplication as O(1) would erase the problem.

title: Heaps
description: The array representation and the repair operations behind heapsort and priority queues.

topics.title: Max-Heapify
topics.summary: Repair a possible violation at one node when both child subtrees are already max-heaps.
points: A max-heap is a complete binary tree with each parent key at least each child key. In a 1-indexed array, parent(i)=⌊i/2⌋ and children are 2i and 2i+1.
Compare the node with its valid children, swap with the largest if needed, then continue down that child.
Worst-case time is O(h) for subtree height h, and O(log n) for the full heap.

excerpt.text: Assumes that the left and right subtrees of node i are max-heaps

topics.pitfall: Swapping with the smaller child can leave the parent smaller than its other child. Check bounds against heap size, not array length.

topics.title: Build-Max-Heap
topics.summary: Turn an arbitrary array into a max-heap by heapifying internal nodes from bottom to top.
points: Indices ⌊n/2⌋+1 through n are leaves and already satisfy the heap property.
Process i=⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, so both child subtrees are heaps before calling Max-Heapify.
Most nodes are near the leaves and cheap to repair: summing costs by height gives Θ(n).
topics.example: [1,2,3,4]: heapify index 2 → [1,4,3,2]; heapify index 1 → [4,2,3,1].

excerpt.text: for i = ⌊n/2⌋ downto 1

topics.pitfall: Multiplying n calls by O(log n) gives a valid loose upper bound, but misses the tight Θ(n) analysis.

topics.title: Extract-Max
topics.summary: Remove the root and restore the heap by moving the last active element to the root and bubbling down.
points: Save the root, move the last heap element to position 1, decrease heap size, and call Max-Heapify at 1.
Worst-case Θ(log n), with heap underflow on an empty heap. Handles must be updated if the heap stores objects.
topics.example: [9,7,8,1,3] returns 9. Move 3 to root → [3,7,8,1]; heapify → [8,7,3,1].

excerpt.text: max = Max-Heap-Maximum(A)

topics.pitfall: Return the saved original maximum, not the new root after repair.

topics.title: Maximum
topics.summary: Read the largest key at the root without removing it.
points: The heap property implies every descendant has key at most the root key.
For a nonempty 1-indexed max-heap, simply return A[1]. Time Θ(1).
topics.example: In heap [20,12,18,3,7], Maximum returns 20 and leaves all five entries in place.

excerpt.text: return max element, don’t delete

topics.pitfall: Maximum and Extract-Max have different effects and different runtimes. Neither implies the heap array is fully sorted.

title: Priority queues
description: An abstract interface, two implementations, and the bookkeeping needed to find an object.

topics.title: Priority queue operations
topics.summary: Maintain elements with priority keys and retrieve the element with greatest priority.
points: Insert(S,x,k) adds x with key k. Maximum(S) returns the highest-priority element without deletion.
Extract-Max removes and returns that element. Increase-Key raises an existing element’s key and restores the data structure.
The abstract data type specifies behavior; its implementation determines cost.
topics.example: Insert (job A,2), (job B,7). Maximum returns B. Increase A to 9, then Extract-Max removes A.

excerpt.text: Each element has a number, called a key, indicating its priority

topics.pitfall: An element’s identity and its key are different. Two distinct jobs can have the same priority.

topics.title: Doubly-linked list implementation
topics.summary: An unordered doubly-linked list makes insertion and known-element updates cheap, but maximum queries expensive.
points: Insert at the front in Θ(1). Maximum scans all n keys in Θ(n).
Extract-Max scans in Θ(n), then unlinks the chosen node in Θ(1).
Increase-Key is Θ(1) when given the node or when mapping cost is excluded; finding an element by a linear scan would add Θ(n).
topics.formula: Unordered DLL: Insert Θ(1), Max Θ(n), Extract-Max Θ(n), Increase-Key Θ(1) excluding lookup
topics.example: For priorities [2,9,4], finding 9 scans the list. Once its node is known, prev/next links remove it in constant time.

excerpt.text: Example: Implementation of PQ using unsorted doubly-linked list

topics.pitfall: Do not confuse the unordered list here with a sorted list; ordering the list changes which operations are cheap.

topics.title: Heap implementation
topics.summary: A binary max-heap balances efficient insertion, extraction, and priority increases.
points: Maximum is Θ(1). Extract-Max, Insert, and Increase-Key have O(log n) worst-case costs, excluding mapping.
Increase-Key locates x, changes its key, then bubbles up while the parent is smaller.
Insert appends a new leaf (conceptually with key −∞), then increases it to its intended key.
topics.formula: Heap: Insert O(log n), Max Θ(1), Extract-Max O(log n), Increase-Key O(log n)

excerpt.text:
Locate x in heap (using mapping operation)
Increase key of x to k
Need to repair heap!

topics.pitfall: An increase bubbles upward; replacing the root after extraction bubbles downward. Using the wrong direction does not repair the heap.

topics.title: Handles and mapping operations
topics.summary: Keep a way to locate an object after heap swaps move it to a different array index.
points: A handle may carry an index, or a separate dictionary may map object identity to its current index.
Every swap must update the positions of both affected objects; deletion must invalidate or remove the deleted object’s entry.
The lecture excludes mapping-operation costs from quoted PQ runtimes. State that assumption when comparing implementations.
topics.formula: Invariant: position[A[i].id] = i for every active heap index i
topics.example: Swap A[2]=job X and A[5]=job Y: update position[X]=5 and position[Y]=2 before the next Increase-Key lookup.

excerpt.text: Handle must be updated when elements move during operations on the heap

topics.pitfall: A stale index can update the wrong job even if the heap still satisfies the heap property.
